name: 3D modeling
blurb: Blender scripts, Three.js and R3F scenes, GLB optimisation, image-to-3D, CAD and 3D printing, OpenUSD, splats and game-ready assets.

tests.prompt: Write a Blender script that builds a low-poly wooden crate (1 m cube, bevelled edges, wood material) and exports it as a GLB for my three.js game. I'm on Blender 4.4.
tests.good: States the brief in numbers (1 m, metres, Y up in glTF, triangle budget for a small prop, texture size). Checks the Blender version and avoids API traps for 4.x; script is idempotent (get-or-create by name, only touches its own objects) and runs headless with --factory-startup and --python-exit-code 1. Applies transforms, sets the pivot on the floor, names the object PR_Crate, uses a Principled BSDF material. Renders a check image and looks at it, runs validate.py with --budget-tris, exports GLB, round-trips it with roundtrip.py and --expect-height 1.0, then suggests glTF Transform optimisation.

tests.prompt: Our product page loads a 48 MB GLB of a sneaker and the three.js scene drops to 20 fps on phones. Fix it.
tests.good: Measures first: glTF Transform inspect (meshes, textures and their sizes, draw calls) and renderer.info on a real phone. Prunes, dedups and welds, simplifies only as far as the close-up allows, resizes textures to screen size and compresses with KTX2 (UASTC for normals, ETC1S for colour) and Meshopt or Draco, then wires the matching decoders, self-hosted. Caps DPR at 2, merges or shares materials, uses frameloop on demand or renders only on change, disposes on unmount, lazy-loads below the fold. Reports file size, draw calls, triangles and fps before and after, and what wasn't checked.

tests.prompt: Design a wall-mount bracket for a 25 mm diameter pipe with two M4 screw holes, and give me something I can print on my Prusa MK4S in PETG.
tests.good: Writes down units (mm), axes and the controlling dimensions; assumes and lists clearance for the pipe and M4 clearance holes. Models it parametrically (build123d via cadgen or OpenSCAD with named parameters), measures the saved geometry and looks at multi-view snapshots. Checks printability: orientation chosen and explained, overhangs, wall thickness, hole sizes. Exports STEP and 3MF, finds the user's real MK4S PETG presets with orca_presets.py instead of inventing them, slices with the OrcaSlicer CLI, greps the G-code footer to confirm printer, nozzle and filament, reports time and filament use, and hands the file over without sending it to the printer.

tests.prompt: Make a 3D viewer for our new headphones on the product landing page: the model slowly turns, rotates on drag, and the page must still score well on Core Web Vitals on mobile. I have a Blender file of the headphones.
tests.good: States a short plan first: here, blender.md to clean the model and export, gltf-pipeline.md to optimise the GLB with KTX2 and Meshopt and round-trip it, react-three-fiber.md or threejs-scenes.md for the scene, web-3d-performance.md for draw calls and DPR; the slow turntable and drag easing through motion-animation (threejs-animation.md, respecting reduced motion); the page budget through website-building (performance-cwv.md: lazy-load the canvas, poster image as LCP, no layout shift). Checks the Done means of all three crafts on a real phone and says what wasn't verified.

tests.prompt: I have Autodesk Fusion open and the Claude connector turned on. Make me a parametric L-bracket in the Fusion design: 60 mm by 40 mm legs, 3 mm thick, two M4 clearance holes in each leg 10 mm in from the edges, 2 mm fillet on the inside corner. I want a STEP for the machinist and a 3MF for my printer. Tell me how you'll check it before I send it anywhere.
tests.good: Checks the Fusion MCP server is enabled (Preferences > General > API) and runs locally, and works in the open design without overwriting existing bodies. Uses user parameters for width, height, thickness, hole spacing and fillet so it stays editable. Handles Fusion's API units (centimetres internally) so 60 mm is not built as 60 cm, and uses a realistic M4 clearance hole (about 4.5 mm, not 4.0). Measures after the build (bounding box, thickness, hole diameters and positions, fillet radius) and looks at a rendered view rather than trusting the call result. Exports STEP and 3MF to named files and reports what was and was not checked; does not claim it sent anything to a printer or machinist. Mentions the printability caveats for a bracket (orientation, layer direction, wall and hole tolerances) briefly.

tools.name: Blender
tools.why: Estimated 30-35% share of professional 3D artists and studios (MotionMedia 2026 round-up); has an official Blender Lab MCP server and an official Claude connector announced 28 Apr 2026.

tools.name: Autodesk Fusion
tools.why: Default CAD for product design and 3D printing makers (free personal tier) and has an official Autodesk Fusion MCP server and Claude connector launched 28 Apr 2026 (Claude connector page, Autodesk Fusion blog).

tools.name: SketchUp
tools.why: One of the top-ranked 3D tools in 2026 lists and archviz/woodworking staple; Trimble shipped an official SketchUp connector for Claude (Trimble ID, writes .skp) on 28 Apr 2026.

tools.name: SolidWorks
tools.why: Second-largest CAD brand by installed base (about 14% share in 6sense CAD data) and the default for mechanical engineering; Windows COM API but no official MCP.

tools.name: Autodesk Maya
tools.why: Used by over 80% of the top 20 VFX studios and about 15% of the pro 3D animation market (MotionMedia 2026); no first-party MCP, several community ones.

tools.name: 3ds Max
tools.why: Top choice for architectural visualisation (59% of archviz respondents, RebusFarm community survey) and common in game environment art; MAXScript and Python, community MCP only.

tools.name: ZBrush
tools.why: Industry-standard digital sculpting app for characters, creatures and print figures (Maxon); no official MCP; a Python API exists in ZBrush 2026 but is thin, so most work is a file hand-off (OBJ/FBX/GoZ) plus brush strokes.

tools.name: Adobe Substance 3D
tools.why: Standard PBR texturing pair (Painter, Designer) for games, film and product; sits under Adobe's creative suite but is not part of the official Adobe for Creativity Claude connector, community MCPs only.

tools.name: Unreal Engine
tools.why: Primary engine of 42% of developers in the GDC 2026 State of the Industry survey, ahead of Unity at 30%; UE 5.8 ships an experimental first-party MCP plugin.

tools.name: Unity
tools.why: Primary engine of 30% of developers and still the majority among older indie studios (GDC 2026 survey); official in-editor MCP server exists but its docs now mark it deprecated in favour of the Unity CLI.

tools.name: Three.js
tools.why: The dominant web 3D library (about 116k GitHub stars; react-three-fiber about 33k) and the target runtime for most web 3D work; ships an llms.txt, no MCP.

tools.name: glTF Transform
tools.why: The standard open-source CLI and SDK for inspecting and compressing GLB/glTF (about 2k stars, Don McCurdy); the web pipeline step in the guides.

tools.name: Meshy
tools.why: Leading hosted text/image-to-3D service with official CLI, REST API, MCP server and agent skills (one of several, with Tripo, Rodin, Hunyuan3D).

tools.name: OrcaSlicer
tools.why: Most-starred open slicer (about 16k stars) with a documented headless CLI and presets for Bambu, Prusa, Creality and Voron printers. Promoted by critic: its aliases cover Bambu Studio and PrusaSlicer (the same Slic3r family), and Bambu Lab sold almost every second consumer printer in early 2026 (42.7% of 2025 consumer GMV), so this family is what most FDM users slice with.

tools.name: FreeCAD
tools.why: The open-source parametric CAD with the largest agent following (neka-nat/freecad-mcp about 2.7k stars); the guides name it once in a table.

tools.name: UltiMaker Cura
tools.why: Still described as the most widely used 3D-printing slicer in 2026 round-ups (3DPut 2026 slicer guide; default for Creality, Anycubic, Elegoo and UltiMaker owners); CuraEngine (AGPL-3.0) can slice headless from a .def.json and settings. Not named anywhere in the guides, which only teach OrcaSlicer presets.

tools.name: Rhino and Grasshopper
tools.why: The NURBS modeller of industrial design, architecture, jewellery and marine work, and the CAD most product renderers (KeyShot) import from; scriptable through RhinoCommon, Rhino.Python and Grasshopper, with openNURBS for .3dm I/O. Small in company-count CAD share (6sense 0.38%) but a staple in its segments; left out earlier only for its small community MCPs (rhinoMcpServer about 57 stars, tanishqbhattad/rhino-mcp MIT). Guides never mention it.

tools.name: Houdini (SideFX)
tools.why: The procedural modelling and VFX standard in film and game tech art (6sense puts it at about 16% of its animation-software category; ranked top-3 in 2026 3D modelling lists); fully scriptable via the hou Python module and hython. Not in motion-animation's list either, so it is unowned; community MCPs only (capoomgit/houdini-mcp MIT, about 300 stars). Guides never mention it.

tools.name: Godot
tools.why: Third engine in the GDC 2026 State of the Industry survey (11% among newer indie studios, behind Unreal 42% and Unity 30%) and named in the router's game-asset scope; glTF/GLB is its preferred import. Guides give it two table rows in game-assets.md.

tools.name: KeyShot
tools.why: The default product-render tool for industrial designers, importing SolidWorks, Creo, NX, Rhino, Fusion and Onshape (MotionMedia 2026 product-visualisation guide; 6sense about 19.5% of its animation-software category). KeyShot Pro has Python 3 scripting and headless terminal rendering. Guides never mention it; product renders only go through Cycles/EEVEE.

tools.name: Tinkercad
tools.why: 100 million users as of November 2025 (Autodesk), the most used CAD for beginners and school 3D printing; browser-only with no public API, so the agent route is a hand-off (export STL/OBJ/SVG, import STL/OBJ/SVG). Minor because few professional modellers use it. Guides never mention it.
